name: Red Hat OpenShift
license: Proprietary subscription (built from open source; the OKD community distribution is Apache 2.0)
summary: Red Hat’s Kubernetes platform: Kubernetes plus its own OS, operators that install and upgrade everything, and stricter security defaults, sold by subscription.
intro: OpenShift Container Platform is a Kubernetes distribution that also owns the layers around it. Every node runs Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS), an image-based, mostly read-only RHEL with the CRI-O runtime, which the cluster updates as one atomic unit through its Machine Config Operator. The platform itself (Kubernetes core services, networking, monitoring, the console, the image registry) is installed and upgraded by operators, which also update Kubernetes and the RHCOS hosts during an over-the-air upgrade. Operator Lifecycle Manager and the OperatorHub catalog install and update further operators, such as databases or a service mesh.

On top of Kubernetes it adds its own APIs and tools: Projects, Routes that publish a Service at a hostname through an HAProxy-based ingress router, a built-in image registry with ImageStreams, Source-to-Image builds, a web console and the `oc` CLI. It is also stricter by default: the `restricted-v2` security context constraint (SCC) drops all Linux capabilities, blocks privilege escalation and runs each container as an arbitrary non-root UID from its project’s range, so images that assume root often need changes.

You can run it yourself, or as a managed service: Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS (ROSA), operated jointly by AWS and Red Hat and billed through AWS, or Azure Red Hat OpenShift (ARO), operated jointly with Microsoft. OKD is the free community distribution built from the same code, now on CentOS Stream CoreOS instead of RHCOS.
strengths: Batteries included: registry, builds, routes, monitoring, console and operator catalog arrive installed and tested together
Over-the-air upgrades for the whole stack, from the node OS to Kubernetes to platform services, driven by operators
Secure defaults (non-root arbitrary UIDs, dropped capabilities, SELinux) that many hand-built clusters lack
One platform self-managed, on ROSA or on ARO, with Red Hat support and an 18-month lifecycle per minor release (longer with Extended Update Support)
limits: Paid: support, certified content and updates come with a Red Hat subscription; OKD is free but has no Red Hat support
Opinionated and large: over 100 operator-managed components, and RHCOS is the only supported OS for any node
Strict SCCs break images that expect to run as root or own their files; they must support an arbitrary UID in the root group
OpenShift-only APIs such as Routes, ImageStreams and Projects can tie manifests and habits to OpenShift

worksWith.how: runs as managed ROSA clusters on

snippet.title: Create a project, run a pod and publish it with a Route
source: oc expose pod/hello-openshift     # creates a Service
oc expose svc hello-openshift     # creates a Route with a hostname on the router

story: OpenShift predates Kubernetes. Red Hat bought Makara, a platform-as-a-service start-up, in late 2010 and launched OpenShift in May 2011 as a hosted PaaS for Ruby, Python, PHP and Java apps. In April 2012 it open-sourced the code as OpenShift Origin under Apache 2.0. Versions 1 and 2 already ran apps in Linux containers, but with Red Hat’s own container runtime and orchestration, in units Red Hat called gears and cartridges.

In 2013 Red Hat bet on Docker for the container format, and in early 2014 it looked for an orchestrator, evaluating Docker’s own efforts, Mesos and a home-grown design. In March 2014 Google showed Red Hat engineers the project that became Kubernetes. Red Hat rebuilt OpenShift on Docker and Kubernetes: Origin 1.0, the code behind OpenShift 3, shipped in June 2015.

In January 2018 Red Hat agreed to buy CoreOS for $250 million, gaining its Container Linux OS, the Tectonic Kubernetes platform and the Quay registry. OpenShift 4, announced in May 2019, combined them: RHCOS replaced general-purpose RHEL nodes, and operators now installed and upgraded the whole platform. The same month Microsoft and Red Hat launched ARO, and AWS and Red Hat followed with ROSA in March 2021.

choices.choice: Adopt Kubernetes instead of keeping its own orchestrator
choices.why: Red Hat compared Docker’s orchestration, Mesos and building its own. It chose Kubernetes for its primitives (pods, services, replication controllers, a real networking model), for Google’s experience with Borg, and for its fast-growing community.

choices.choice: Make the OS part of the cluster
choices.why: OpenShift 4 delivers RHCOS as an immutable host image installed as a component of the cluster. The same operator-driven upgrade then covers the host and Kubernetes, and an OS update that goes wrong rolls back with a single reboot.

OpenShift is many containerized components. Encoding how to install and upgrade each one in an operator turned installs and upgrades of the platform, Kubernetes included, into an automated, over-the-air process.

choices.choice: Arbitrary non-root user IDs by default
choices.why: Running every container as a random UID from the project’s range, not root, limits what a process can do if it escapes the container through a runtime bug. The cost is that images must work as any user.

timeline.text: Red Hat acquires Makara, the PaaS start-up behind the first OpenShift
OpenShift launches in May as a hosted PaaS with its own container system
Code released as OpenShift Origin under Apache 2.0 in April
Origin 1.0, the code base of OpenShift 3, rebuilt on Docker and Kubernetes (June)
Red Hat agrees to buy CoreOS (January); Origin renamed OKD (August)
OpenShift 4 with RHCOS and operator-driven upgrades; Azure Red Hat OpenShift GA
Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS (ROSA) GA in March
OKD 5.0 ships on CentOS Stream CoreOS 10 and Kubernetes 1.36
